samples.summary: `ENTITY_REFERENCE` only refuses semicolon-terminated references, so `&#106avascript:alert(1)` (numeric reference with no `;`) passes the gate and is decoded to `javascript:` by the HTML tokenizer
samples.evidence: `ENTITY_REFERENCE = /&(?:#[0-9]+|#[xX][0-9A-Fa-f]+|[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*);/` (markdown.ts:299) requires a terminating `;`. An attacker-supplied `href` of `&#106avascript:alert(1)` (from HTML paste, DOCX import, or a collaborator's CRDT write) contains only URI characters (`&`, `#`, digits, letters, `:`, `(`, `)`), so `URI_CHARS` accepts it; `ENTITY_REFERENCE` does not match (no `;`); `HAS_SCHEME` (`^[A-Za-z]...`) does not match because the string starts with `&`, so `isEmittableUrl` (markdown.ts:375-379) takes the relative branch and returns true. The exported `.md` therefore contains `[click me](&#106avascript:alert\(1\))`. CommonMark itself will not decode the reference (its spec requires the semicolon), but the destination is then written into an HTML `href` attribute, and the HTML5 tokenizer's *numeric* character-reference path decodes a reference with a missing semicolon (the `next char is = or alphanumeric` suppression rule applies only to *named* references). Any renderer that does not itself escape `&` when emitting the href therefore yields `href="javascript:alert(1)"` — script execution when the exported document is opened. Exploitability depends on the downstream renderer escaping `&` (cmark and marked do), which is why confidence is low; the fix is to drop the `;` requirement for the `&#`/`&#x` forms, or to refuse any `&` not spelled `%26`. Note the new test table (packages/docs/test/serialize/markdown.test.ts:758-763) covers only the semicolon-terminated spellings, so nothing in CI exercises this form.

samples.summary: `escapeMarkdownText` does not escape the line-leading block markers `#`, `>`, `-`, `+`, `|`, or `N.`, so a run at the start of a block can forge document structure in the exported `.md`
samples.evidence: `escapeMarkdownText` escapes only `[\\*_[\]`~<]` (markdown.ts:472). A paragraph block whose text is `# Forged heading`, `> quoted`, `- item`, or `| a | b |` is emitted verbatim at the start of a line by `blockToMarkdown` (markdown.ts:112-113) and renders as a heading / blockquote / list / table row rather than as literal text. The run content is attacker-influenceable through the same channels the diff already identifies for `href` and `alt` (HTML paste, DOCX import, a collaborator's CRDT write). This is markdown *structure* injection only — `<` is escaped, so it does not reach raw HTML or script — and the newline fold added by this change means the forgery is limited to the first run of a block. The new test at markdown.test.ts:547 (`intro  # Forged heading`) only demonstrates the mid-line case, which is inherently safe; the line-leading case is untested. Behaviour predates this change, but this function is exactly what the change hardens.

samples.summary: `safeFilename`, now extended to `md`/`txt`, strips only `\ / : * ? " < > |` — control characters, newlines, bidi overrides and a leading dot survive into the `download` attribute
samples.evidence: `safeFilename` (export-utils.ts:110) applies `.replace(/[\\/:*?"<>|]+/g, "_")` and nothing else, then `downloadBlob` sets `a.download = filename` (export-utils.ts:65). A document title controlled by any collaborator can carry `‮` (RTL override) to display a `.txt` download as e.g. `gpj.exe`, or C0 control characters / a leading `.` to produce a dotfile. The diff widens the extension union to `"md" | "txt"`, so the helper now serves two more download paths. The task doc at docs/tasks/active/20260829-docs-surface-existing-features-todo.md:106-109 records this as a known pre-existing limitation for `.pdf`/`.docx`; it is not introduced here, but the blast radius grows with the new entry points. Browsers do sanitize `download` to a degree, which is why confidence is not high.

samples.summary: `URI_CHARS` admits the whole `-￿` range, so invisible/bidi characters (U+200B, U+2060, U+202E) are accepted inside an emitted link destination
samples.evidence: `URI_CHARS` (markdown.ts:282) admits every non-ASCII code unit, and `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` (markdown.ts:263) only catches the subset JavaScript's `\s` treats as whitespace plus C0/C1. U+200B (zero-width space), U+2060 (word joiner) and U+202E (right-to-left override) are in neither class, so an attacker-supplied `href` such as `https://good.example‮/moc.live//:sptth` is emitted verbatim and can misrepresent its own target in a renderer's status bar or link preview. The admission is deliberate (so `/uploads/한글.png` survives), and the impact is display spoofing rather than code execution, hence nit severity. Worth considering an explicit refusal of the Cf general category.

verdict.reason: Verified independently in the repository; the finding is accurate. (1) markdown.ts:299 is exactly as quoted, with a mandatory terminating ';' in all three alternatives. (2) I hand-traced `&#106avascript:alert(1)`: UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS (263) passes (no whitespace/controls); URI_CHARS (282) passes (&, #, digits, letters, :, parens are all RFC 3986 URI chars); ENTITY_REFERENCE does not match — the numeric branch consumes `#106` then requires ';' but finds 'a', no shorter backtrack succeeds, and the named branch cannot start on '#' — so isLiteralDestination (328-333) returns true. HAS_SCHEME (349) is anchored ^[A-Za-z] and the string starts with '&', so isEmittableUrl (375-379) takes the relative branch, SCHEME_RELATIVE (359) does not match, and it returns true. (3) escapeMarkdownHref (506-508) replaces only parentheses and never escapes '&', so line 225 emits the payload verbatim into the .md. (4) No guard elsewhere: the only call sites (224, 400, 420) all funnel through the same isLiteralDestination. (5) The gap contradicts the module's own documented invariant (320-323) that it refuses any destination having a decoder rewrite to apply, since the HTML5 numeric character-reference path decodes without a semicolon (the alphanumeric-suppression rule governs only named references). (6) The coverage claim is correct: DECODED_PAYLOADS (746-767) lists only semicolon-terminated spellings, so the strong assertion at line 776 never exercises this form. No refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, nothing guards it, and XSS/injection sanitization in an export path is squarely in the security lane. Full exploitation depends on a downstream renderer failing to escape '&', which justifies major rather than critical severity but does not refute the weakness — doubt about exploitability belongs in confidence, not in dropping the finding.

finding.summary: Markdown URL gate lets `<` / `>` through, enabling an angle-bracket link-destination bypass and raw-HTML injection into the exported `.md`
finding.evidence:
`isEmittableUrl()` (markdown.ts:295-300) refuses whitespace/C0-C1 controls and then routes on `HAS_SCHEME = /^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9+.-]*:/`. A destination that *starts with* `<` never matches `HAS_SCHEME`, so it is classified as a harmless relative reference and emitted verbatim (`escapeMarkdownHref`, line 396, escapes only `\` and `)` — never `<` or `>`, even though `escapeMarkdownText` at line 374 does escape `<` in body text precisely because it is dangerous).

Attacker path (identical provenance to the one the diff's own comments cite: HTML paste, DOCX/HTML import, a collaborator's CRDT write into `style.href` / `image.src`), then victim exports via the new Export → Markdown entry (`packages/frontend/src/app/docs/text-actions.ts:44`) or `wafflebase docs content --format md`:

1. `href = "<javascript:alert(1)>"` → gate passes → output `[t](<javascript:alert\(1\)>)`. CommonMark's first link-destination form is "a sequence of characters between an opening `<` and a closing `>`", with backslash escapes processed, so the rendered href is exactly `javascript:alert(1)` — the one value the whole gate exists to block.
2. `href = "<script>alert(1)</script>"` (no whitespace, so `UNEMITTABLE_URL_CHARS` does not fire) → output `[t](<script>alert\(1\)</script>)`. The link fails to parse (destination `<script>` is not followed by whitespace/`)`), the run degrades to literal text, and `<script>`/`</script>` are then re-parsed as CommonMark *inline raw HTML* — so the exported document renders `<script>alert(1)</script>` in any renderer that does not strip HTML.
3. The same `<…>` wrapper defeats the image gate: `src = "<data:text/html;base64,…>"` fails both `/^data:/i` (so the `inlineImages:false` placeholder branch is skipped, markdown.ts:330) and `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` (line 309), yet `isSafeImageSrc` returns true via the relative branch.

No test covers `<` in an href/src (test/serialize/markdown.test.ts:552-720 covers only schemes, scheme-relative `//`/`\\`, and whitespace/contro

verdict.reason: The described code is not present. `isEmittableUrl` (markdown.ts:375-379) does not route from the control-char check straight to HAS_SCHEME; its first statement is `if (!isLiteralDestination(url)) return false;` (:376). `isLiteralDestination` (:328-333) applies an anchored RFC-3986 allowlist `URI_CHARS` (:282, enforced at :331) whose character class `[A-Za-z0-9\-._~:/?#[\]@!$&'()*+,;=%-￿]` contains neither `<` nor `>` nor `\`. All three claimed payloads are therefore rejected: `<javascript:alert(1)>` and `<script>alert(1)</script>` fail URI_CHARS so the href degrades to plain text (:224-226), and `<data:text/html;base64,...>` is refused because `isSafeImageSrc` (:392-401) calls `isLiteralDestination(src)` at :399 BEFORE testing SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI or isEmittableUrl, so `imageInline` returns `[image]` (:420-422). The entity variant `javascript:` is likewise refused by ENTITY_REFERENCE (:299, applied :332). The claim that `escapeMarkdownHref` failing to escape `<`/`>` is exploitable does not hold because its only two call sites (:225, :423) are both behind that allowlist. The finding's cited line numbers (295-300, 396, 374, 330, 309) do not match the actual definitions (375, 506, 469, 413, 389), and the file's comment at :309-312 explicitly names this angle-bracket bypass as the reason the literal-destination gate was added — the finding describes a superseded revision.

finding.summary: HTML entity references let a dangerous scheme through the `HAS_SCHEME` → `isSafeUrl` split, because CommonMark decodes entities inside link destinations
finding.evidence:
`isEmittableUrl` only sends a reference to `isSafeUrl` when the *raw* string matches `HAS_SCHEME` (line 271/298); anything else is accepted as "cannot name a protocol". But CommonMark explicitly recognizes entity and numeric character references inside link destinations (spec example `[foo](/föö)` → `href="/föö"`).

So an attacker-supplied `style.href` of `javascript:alert(1)` starts with `&`, does not match `HAS_SCHEME`, does not match `SCHEME_RELATIVE`, contains no whitespace or controls → emitted verbatim as `[text](javascript:alert(1))`. A CommonMark renderer decodes it to `javascript:alert(1)` and, unless it applies its own scheme sanitizer, produces a live `javascript:` link in a document exported from Wafflebase. The same trick reproduces the scheme-relative case the diff deliberately blocks: `//evil.example/x` decodes to `//evil.example/x`, and it also reaches the image path via `isSafeImageSrc` (line 318). The gate's own premise — "with no scheme they cannot select a dangerous one" (comment at line 291-293) — does not hold once the consumer decodes entities.

verdict.reason: The described gap does not exist in the working tree. `markdown.ts:299` defines `ENTITY_REFERENCE = /&(?:#[0-9]+|#[xX][0-9A-Fa-f]+|[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9]*);/`, and `isLiteralDestination` (markdown.ts:328-333) rejects any destination matching it at line 332. `isEmittableUrl` (markdown.ts:375-379) calls `isLiteralDestination` at line 376 BEFORE the `HAS_SCHEME` -> `isSafeUrl` split (line 377) and before the `SCHEME_RELATIVE` check (line 378), so both claimed payloads fail: `javascript:alert(1)` matches `j` and `//evil.example/x` matches `/`, both returning false at line 332 without ever reaching the scheme logic. The image path is equally covered: `isSafeImageSrc` (markdown.ts:392-401) calls `isLiteralDestination(src)` at line 399 before both `SAFE_IMAGE_DATA_URI` and `isEmittableUrl`. Both and only these two emission sites exist (href at markdown.ts:224-225, image at markdown.ts:420-423). The finding's cited line numbers (271/298, 291-293, 318) do not match this file, and the doc comments at markdown.ts:284-298 and 308-317 explicitly name CommonMark entity decoding as the transform being closed -- the finding describes a prior revision ("round 3", referenced at line 305), not the current code.
